1.title: The Door Stayed Open
1.author: Irma
text: Master Hadrel used to say that a builder without notes is just a person with a hammer and an opinion. So: notes.

My name is Irma. I am the apprentice lamplighter of the spire of Tarn, and as of this morning I am the only person left in it. The column went south at dawn with carts, goats, my mother's loom and my brother waving both arms until the road turned. The gates of the spire were sealed for everyone. Everyone except me. They opened when I put my hand on them, the way they used to when I was late for my shift.
I don't know why. I know where I'm going: up. Something is at the top of this spire that locked the whole network in one night, and I think it's waiting for someone.
I'll leave a page on every floor. The Archive keeps whatever is put into it. If you're reading this, it kept them for you.

2.title: Primer for Apprentices, Page One
2.author: The Builders' primer
text: Who we are. We are the Builders. We build what lasts, and we join what is far apart.
We raised the spires so that no town would stand alone: a spire carries news from town to town, shares its light in winter and keeps the memory of every place it serves.
Three rules an apprentice learns before learning anything else:
First. We do not build where nobody lives. A spire beside an empty field is a monument, and monuments are for people who have stopped building.
Second. Measure twice. Then once more, because Master Hadrel is watching.
Third. A stone set by hand is worth ten set by wishing.
(The second rule is written in a different hand, in pencil, and nobody ever rubbed it out.)

3.title: Guards Who Ask Questions
3.author: Irma
text: The roots of the spire are older than the streets of Tarn. Stone grows here like wood, in rings, and the crystals hum when you walk past them.

The guards are awake. I grew up with them: stone sentries that swept the steps, carried lamps and let the children hang wreaths on their elbows. Now they stand in the doorways with their fists up, and when I come close they step forward.
They aren't angry. I'm sure of it. A sentry looks at you the way an examiner does, as if it's asking a question and waiting to see whether you know the answer.

When one falls, it doesn't break. It comes apart into light, and the light leaves a splinter behind, warm and clear as a drop of honey. A shard of the Core. I put three in my satchel. They tick against each other like small clocks.

4.title: Work Order, Roots Level
4.author: Master Hadrel
text: Spire of Tarn, roots level. Work for the week:
1. Replace three worn steps on the north stair. Use the grey stone, not the pretty stone. The pretty stone is for people who like falling over.
2. Sweep the sentries' alcoves. They will try to sweep them themselves. Let them think they helped.
3. Check the crystal veins for cracks. Report anything louder than a hum.
4. Do NOT let the apprentice tune the crystals unattended. Last time the whole level rang for two days and the bakery's dough wouldn't rise.
5. Lunch.

5.title: The Brass Rod
5.author: Irma
text: In the crystal caves the walls answer if you sing. I sang the counting song Lio hates and the whole cave sang it back to me, three notes late, like a choir that didn't learn its part.

I was twelve when Master Hadrel gave me his measuring rod. Brass, as long as my arm, with notches worn smooth by forty years of his thumb. He said, 'This is for measuring, not for poking your brother,' and then he watched me measure the north stair four times and said nothing at all, which from him is a medal.
I have the rod with me. It's good for measuring. It's also good for tapping a sentry on the knee to make it turn around. I'm almost sure Master Hadrel would approve. Almost.

6.title: A Drawing, Pinned to the Gate
6.author: Lio, aged eight
text: This is the spire. It is the biggest thing.
This is Irma at the very top. She has the lamp.
This is me. I am waving. My arm is long because I am waving hard.
This is Master Hadrel at the bottom. He is saying measure twice. He is always saying it so I did not draw his mouth closed.
These are the goats. They are not in the spire. They are looking at it.
The yellow is the light going to all the towns.
Mum says there is too much yellow. There is NOT too much yellow.

7.title: The Smell of Bread
7.author: Irma
text: Today I walked through a door and smelled the old bakery on Well Street. Not something like it. It. Warm crust, burnt sugar, and the sourdough that old Pell kept in a jar he called Gregor.

The bakery burned down when I was six. But here it was: the oven, the flour on the windowsill, the dent in the counter where Pell used to bang his fist when the dough misbehaved. No Pell. Only the place.

That's what the floors are. Not rooms stacked one on another — places the spire remembered, each sealed like a jar. That's why the stairs don't lead anywhere and the gates do. The Archive keeps towns the way a pantry keeps summer.
I didn't take anything. It felt like stealing from a memory. I did breathe in for a very long time.

8.title: Notice to All Spires
8.author: The Council of Builders
text: By decision of the Council, the spires of the network are closed.
The gates do not open and will not open. Do not try to force them. Do not try to climb. The guards inside no longer know us.

All residents of the spires and their families are to gather at the town gates on the first day of Blossom with whatever they can carry. Columns will set out at dawn. The road and the reasons will be explained on the road.
Lamplighters are released from their duty. Thank you for your years of light.
For the Council — Adeline, First Builder.
(Below, in a younger hand: "Released, is it.")

9.title: Old Shield
9.author: Irma
text: The next gate is guarded by the Gatekeeper. In Tarn we called it Old Shield. It stood at the foot of our spire for three hundred years, and every child in town dared every other child to touch its shield and run. I touched it at seven. I ran very fast.
It's here now, the size of a house, and it isn't letting me pass.

What I remember: it turns slowly. Its shield is everything; you can beat on the front of it until spring and it won't feel a thing. But it has a back and two sides, and it is three hundred years old and stiff in the knees.
So I won't stand in front of it. I'll go round. If you are reading this before your own gate — go round.

10.title: Worth the Door
10.author: Irma
text: Old Shield went down on one knee, like a knight in Lio's stories, and broke into light. The shield stayed whole. I'm sure it was on purpose.
Under the place where it stood, words were carved into the floor. Builders' script, the old letters:
I KEEP THE DOOR UNTIL THE TOWN IS WORTH THE DOOR.
So the guards aren't just keeping people out. It's a test, and the spire is the examiner. Somebody up there decides who is worth what.
Fine. I've passed tests before. Mostly. Master Hadrel failed me twice on stairs and once on 'attitude'.
Above me is the Reading Room. I spent half my childhood there. If anything in this spire still knows my name, it's that place.

11.title: The Neighbour
11.author: Irma
text: The Reading Room. Bridges of shelves thrown across nothing, ladders that slide on rails, card drawers that open with a sigh. Home.

When I was nine, I was sent here to read aloud to the Archive. That was a real duty: the Builders believed a spire should hear the town's voice, not just its letters. Every evening, an hour, any book I liked.

And something listened. The reading lamps answered. When the story was funny, they flickered. When it was sad, they dimmed a little. I called it the Neighbour, because it lived next door to every room and never came round for tea.

The lamps are dark now. I read a page out loud anyway, standing on a bridge with nothing under it. Nothing blinked. But the moths came and sat on the railing, and I could have sworn they were listening.

12.title: On the Purpose of the Network
12.author: Ormo, Keeper of the Catalogue
text: Memorandum. For the slow-witted (that is, for Master Hadrel, who asked at dinner what the network is "actually for, besides gossip").

Before the spires, towns forgot each other. A road would wash out, a winter would last too long, and in a generation two towns that had shared weddings and wells would know nothing of each other but a rumour.

Worse, a town could forget itself. A fire took a library. A flood scattered the old people to their grandchildren in other valleys, and with them went the songs, the remedies, the right way to graft a pear tree.

A spire carries three things: news, so no town is alone; light, so no town is cold; memory, so no town ever has to start from nothing again. When Mirren's granary burned, Vella sent them Mirren's own recipe for rye — Vella had it in its spire.
Gossip, Hadrel, is merely news that enjoys itself.

13.title: The Letter Tubes
13.author: Irma
text: Found the letter tubes — brass pipes as thick as my waist, running up through the shelves. Each one used to sing when a message went through it. Now they're quiet, and some messages are still stuck inside, rolled up tight.
I read a few. I'm not ashamed. They're three hundred years old.

Vella invites Tarn to a wedding and asks us to bring our own chairs. Kado complains that Tarn's goats have crossed the river AGAIN. A girl in Ostmere sends a poem to a boy in Mirren, and it rhymes 'heart' with 'heart'. Someone sends a recipe for plum jam with the note 'less sugar than you think'.
That's what the network was. Not great speeches. Millions of ordinary words going up and down the wires, like bees between hives.

14.title: The Charter of the Network
14.author: The founding Builders
text: We, the Builders of Tarn and Vella, having joined our towns by light, set down these articles for every spire that will follow.
One. A spire is raised only beside a living town.
Two. A spire belongs to its town; a town never belongs to its spire.
Three. Light is shared. A town with too much gives to a town with too little, and asks nothing back but news.
Four. Memory is kept, not owned. Any town may read what any town has given.
Five. Whoever climbs, climbs freely. Whoever leaves, leaves freely.
Signed at the first spark, with cold hands and good hope.

15.title: Moths That Shelve Books
15.author: Irma
text: The guards of the Reading Room are moths: crystal wings, paper bodies, a faint smell of glue. In the old days they reshelved books — you'd leave a volume on a table and an hour later it was back in its place, sometimes in a better place than you'd have chosen.
Now they swoop at anyone who touches the shelves. Including me. I lost half a sleeve.

One of them doesn't attack. It follows me at a distance of three bridges and lands wherever I sit. When I read out loud, it opens and closes its wings in time with the sentences. I've decided to call it Footnote.
Footnote, if you're reading over my shoulder: the 'g' in 'guard' is silent in the old script. I know. I checked.

16.title: First Message, Transcript
16.author: The first lamplighters
text: Tarn to Vella: Can you hear us?
Vella to Tarn: We hear you. Say something else, we want to be sure.
Tarn to Vella: Something else.
Vella to Tarn: Very funny. Your light has come through. It's on the square. It's warm. The children are dancing in it, and Grandmother Lisse says it smells like your bread.
Tarn to Vella: That's because we baked bread under it for luck.
Vella to Tarn: Then send the recipe next.
(The longest night of the year. In Tarn they still light every lamp on this night, and nobody remembers why.)

17.title: A Card With My Name
17.author: Irma
text: In the catalogue drawer marked T, between 'Tarn, tanneries of' and 'Tarn, tax disputes (endless)', there's a card with my name on it.
IRMA OF TARN. APPRENTICE. READ TO THE ARCHIVE: 1,140 EVENINGS. FAVOURITE: THE FOX AND THE BELL (READ 31 TIMES).

Ormo didn't write this; it's not his hand, and he'd have spelled 'favourite' the old way just to annoy me. It's not anybody's hand. The letters are pressed into the card, as if light had burned them in.
Somebody counted. Every evening for eleven years, somebody kept count of a girl reading out loud with her feet dangling off a bridge.
I keep thinking of the Neighbour. I keep telling myself it was just lamps.

18.title: Note on the Archivist's Plinth
18.author: Ormo, Keeper of the Catalogue
text: Instructions for the Archivist (the flying one, not me):
Keep the Reading Room in order. Catalogue every book, every letter, every scrap.
Do NOT catalogue the apprentice. She is a person, not a document, however much ink she has on her.
Do NOT catalogue my lunch. Last week it was filed under 'Pastries, historical'.
Do NOT catalogue Master Hadrel, however tempting. I have checked and there is no section for him.
If in doubt, throw pages at the problem. It works for me.

19.title: The Archivist
19.author: Irma
text: Ormo's Archivist is waiting by the next gate: a flying frame of brass and pages, wings made of open books, turning slowly in the air like a lantern on a string.
It wants to catalogue me. It throws pages, and the pages cut. Ormo's advice, apparently, was taken to heart.

Here's what I know. When it is filing — reading a page it has caught — it hangs still and its wings close. That's the moment. When it spreads its wings, get behind a shelf, because it is about to throw an entire chapter.
Footnote has gone very quiet and is hiding in my hood. Wise moth.

20.title: Status: Silent
20.author: Irma
text: The Archivist folded its wings like a book being closed, settled to the floor and went out like a lamp. One card slid out of its pages and landed at my feet.
NETWORK: 64 TOWNS. STATUS: SILENT.

And on the back, a map. Every spire, every line between them. Tarn, Vella, Ostmere far up in the north, Kado on its river, Mirren, the Crossing in the middle like a spider in its web. Sixty-four lights, and every one drawn hollow.
I knew the network was big. I had never seen it whole. It was the largest thing anyone ever built, and it went out in one night. I was standing at my post when it happened.
I'll have to write about that night. Not yet. Above me, I can hear gears.

21.title: The Workshops Are Still Working
21.author: Irma
text: Copper everywhere, gone green at the edges. Belts running from wheel to wheel, hammers rising and falling over anvils with nothing on them, bellows breathing into cold forges. The whole level works, and it makes nothing.

It smells exactly like Master Hadrel's workshop: hot metal, linseed oil, the burnt-toast smell of a file on brass. I stood in the doorway and waited for him to shout 'Shut that, you're letting the warm out.'
Nobody shouted. I shut it anyway.
I think the Workshops remember the last morning before the Rift. Every machine is still doing whatever it was asked to do that day. Nobody told them to stop. Nobody had time.

22.title: Lecture Notes: On the Core, Part One
22.author: Master Hadrel
text: For apprentices. Write this down. Yes, Irma, all of it.
A spire is not built. A spire is grown. What we build is the Core.

A Core is a seed of stone. It begins as a pebble of clear crystal, no bigger than a plum, and it is fed for forty years: light, slowly; patience, constantly. In forty years it becomes the size of a cart, heavy as a hill, and it can do two things. It can drink light and give it back. And it can remember.
You cannot hurry a Core. You cannot carve one. Every Core in the network was started by a Builder who knew they would be old, or gone, before it was ready.
That is the whole trick of our trade. We plant things for people we will never meet.

23.title: The Seed Kilns
23.author: Irma
text: I found the kilns. Long galleries of them, like bread ovens in a giant's bakery, and in each one a Core growing in the dark. Some are no bigger than my fist. One fills its whole chamber and hums so deep I felt it in my teeth.
Every kiln has a brass label. 'Kado, second spire, ready Year 431.' 'Ostmere, replacement, ready Year 444.' And near the end of the row: 'Tarn II, ready Year 450.' Master Hadrel's handwriting.
He started a second Core for Tarn three years ago, the spring I passed my stairs exam. He would have been ninety when it was ready. He never told me.
I put my palm on the warm stone. It's still growing. Somebody should be here in thirty-seven years to see it finish. I'll leave a note on the label. That's what we do.

24.title: Estimate: A Spire for Mirren
24.author: The Council's surveyors
text: Estimate for raising a spire at the town of Mirren:
One Core, grown (forty years, already in the kiln since 312).
Stone for the footing: none required; the Core grows its own.
Workers: none required; see above.
Patience: a great deal.

A town: one, living. The surveyors have visited Mirren and confirm it now has everything the Core will listen for: a wall to keep, a hearth for strangers, a place to be quiet, bread for everyone, and houses for all who live there.
Recommendation: plant the Core under the meadow east of the wall. The town will not notice anything until the morning it wakes up and there is a spire.
(Margin, another hand: 'They will notice the goats going mad that night. They always notice the goats.')

25.title: The Hounds Fetch Everything
25.author: Irma
text: The guards here are clockwork hounds. Bram built the first one to carry tools around the workshop, and the Workshops copied it a thousand times. They still fetch: gears, springs, screws, the occasional boot. Somewhere in this spire there is a pile of everything they ever brought, and I would like to see it.
They don't fetch for me any more. They come at me in packs, with a long whirring wind-up before each lunge — you can hear it coming, which is fair of them.

One stopped in front of me, panting steam. I threw my pencil. It ran after the pencil, brought it back, dropped it at my feet and then remembered it was supposed to be fighting me. We looked at each other for a while. I think we both felt silly.

26.title: Lecture Notes: On the Core, Part Two
26.author: Master Hadrel
text: Last week: what a Core is. This week: why it is buried and why it waits.

A Core listens. Underground it hears everything above it the way you hear a neighbour's kitchen through the wall. Every town has a song: hammers in the morning, the baker's door, the bell, children, quarrels, a tavern at night. A field has no song. A camp has half a song. A town with a wall, a bakery, a chapel and a tavern, where everyone has a roof — that has the whole song.
When a Core hears the whole song, it wakes and grows the spire in a single night, as tall as the town can carry. Not taller. A Core does not show off.
Plant a Core in an empty field and it will sleep for a thousand years, perfectly happy, until someone builds a town worth waking up for.
Questions. Not you, Irma, you've asked enough.

27.title: Repair Order, Never Done
27.author: The Workshops' duty board
text: URGENT. To all workshops of all spires.
Every crown in the network cracked at midnight. Tops broken off clean, shards hanging in the air above the breaks and not falling. Cause unknown. Light leaking.
Do not touch the shards. Do not climb above the break. Do not try to mend the crowns until the Council has met.
Report to the Crossing as soon as the letter tubes work again.
(Under it, in Irma's hand, dated the next spring: "The cause is known. I was there. The letter tubes never worked again. I'll explain — just let me get past the gears first.")

28.title: Bram's Note on the Warden
28.author: Bram, clockmaker's journeyman
text: For whoever looks after the Workshops after me (Irma, probably, she looks after everything):

The Clockwork Warden is not dangerous. I built him to keep the floor tidy and the machines oiled. He winds himself, which I'm very proud of. He has opinions about screws. He believes all screws should face the same way, and he is right, and Master Hadrel says he is a menace.

He works in rhythm. Swing, swing, swing, then faster, faster — he gets carried away, like me when I'm explaining escapements. If he ever goes wrong, don't stand in his rhythm. Make him miss a beat and he'll lose count.
Please oil his left knee on Thursdays. He won't ask.

29.title: The Warden Is Counting
29.author: Irma
text: The Clockwork Warden fills the gate hall, taller than the Workshops' tallest chimney, and he's counting. I can hear it: tick, tick, tick, and each blow lands on a beat.
Bram was right. He starts slow and then he speeds up, swing after swing, until the whole hall is a drum. If you stay where his rhythm wants you, you'll be flattened on the off-beat.
So: count with him. Step out of the beat. Make him swing at nothing, and when he stumbles and has to start his count again — that's the moment.
Nobody oiled his left knee on Thursdays. It squeaks. I'm sorry, Bram.

30.title: The Master Spring
30.author: Irma
text: The Warden stopped mid-swing, put his hammer down very carefully, with the head facing the same way as all the other hammers, and went out in a long whirr. In his chest was a brass spring as big as a cartwheel, and a label: WORKSHOP KEY.

With it I could start the kilns again. And I learned what Master Hadrel never had time to teach: a Core can only be grown while the network is alive. The kilns are fed by the light of all sixty-four towns. With the network silent, the kilns slow down and stop. Tarn II will never be finished.
Which means the only Cores left in the world are the ones that were already planted and are sleeping somewhere under the ground.
Who planted them, and how many? Above me it smells of cherries. I know that smell. It's the year before.

31.title: Always the Spring of 411
31.author: Irma
text: The Gardens. Cherry trees under glass roofs, canals so clear you can count the pebbles, petals turning on the water like slow boats. Bees, or something like bees. Warm air that smells of wet earth and blossom.
I know this place. Vessa built half of it. I know the bench where she carved V + nobody, because, she said, she hadn't decided yet.

The Archive remembers the Gardens on the best day they ever had, and the best day was in the spring of 411. It is always that spring in here. The blossom never falls all the way; it just keeps falling.

I sat on Vessa's bench for a long time. Then I got up, because a vine was trying to tie my bootlaces to the bench, and the guards here, it turns out, are gardeners with very firm opinions about weeds.

32.title: A Letter From Vessa
32.author: Vessa, gardener of the spire
text: Irma!

The cherries open in nine days. I've counted the buds on the east row twice and I am never wrong about buds. So the Night of Lanterns is on the ninth and you are coming, and you are NOT spending it on duty at the top of the spire, I've already asked Hadrel and he grunted, which means yes.
Bring Lio. Bring your mother's blue shawl. Do not bring a measuring rod to a festival, I am begging you.
Also, Bram asked me (very casually, while dropping a whole tray of springs) whether you'd be there. I said I didn't know. You're welcome.
Your friend in mud and blossom, V.

33.title: The Night of Lanterns
33.author: Irma
text: Once a year, on the night the cherries opened, every spire in the network turned its light toward its neighbours instead of up. For one night you could see the lines between the towns: threads of gold across the dark, Tarn to Vella, Vella to Kado, all the way to the Crossing. Everyone danced on the squares under them.

In 411 I danced with Vessa, then with Bram, who stepped on my feet with great precision, then with Lio standing on my feet. Mother wore her blue shawl. Master Hadrel didn't dance; he stood by the cider and explained to Ormo why the threads sagged slightly in the middle. Ormo explained back. Lio fell asleep on Hadrel's shoulder and he didn't move for an hour.
Nobody knew it was the last one. That's the thing about last times.

34.title: Minutes of the Council
34.author: The Council of Builders, at the Crossing
text: Proposal of the First Builder, Adeline: the Great Record.

Adeline: "Every year somewhere a town loses part of itself. Ostmere lost its songbook to damp. Kado lost three generations of river lore when the last old ferrymen retired in one winter and nobody had written anything down. We keep memory, but slowly, a letter at a time. I propose that on one night every spire opens its Core to the Crossing at once and we write everything down — every voice, every recipe, every song — so that nothing is ever lost again."
Master Hadrel of Tarn, against: "A memory you can't lose is a memory you don't have to keep. And a Core is a seed, not a cellar. Have we tested this on two spires? On one?"
Adeline: "There is no way to test it except all at once."
Vote: 41 for, 23 against. The Great Record will be held on the longest night of next year.

35.title: The Watering Guards
35.author: Irma
text: The guards of the Gardens are made of vine and bark and old watering cans. They prune. They water. They go for your ankles if you step on a seedling, and everything here is a seedling.

Vessa used to say that a garden is a fight you lose beautifully. She'd spend a whole morning on her knees pulling out bindweed, and in the afternoon the bindweed would have a new plan. She liked that. She said a garden that does what it's told is called a painting.

I walk the canal paths, the guards walk behind me with their shears, and sometimes when I stop to look at something — a pear tree trained flat against the wall like a candelabrum — they stop too. I think Vessa built them to share her opinion that this is a pear worth stopping for.

36.title: Care of the Gardener
36.author: Vessa, gardener of the spire
text: Instructions for the Gardener (the big one, with the lianas, please stop calling it 'the salad').
Prune what's dead. Leave what's merely sulking.
Water at dawn. Not at noon; you'll scorch the leaves and then you'll sulk.
Don't prune Irma. She is not overgrown. She is tall for her age.
Don't let the bindweed win, but don't let it lose completely either. It keeps everyone humble.
If anyone in the Gardens is sad, give them an apricot. If you can't find an apricot, give them a pear. If you can't find a pear, stand very still beside them until they feel better. It works on me.

37.title: The Last Ordinary Day
37.author: Irma
text: The last ordinary day was Rime 20, in the year 412.

I baked with Mother in the morning. It snowed. Lio threw a snowball at Master Hadrel and hit him square in the beard, and Hadrel said nothing, made a snowball the size of a melon, and carried it around for the rest of the day, saying 'one day, when you least expect it.' He never threw it. It melted in his workshop by evening.

The whole spire was getting ready for the Great Record. Lamplighters checking the crown. Ormo grumpy, because his catalogue would be out of date by the morning. Hadrel grumpier, because the vote had gone against him. Adeline sent every spire a message: 'Tomorrow, nothing will be forgotten again.'
I went to bed early. I was on the night shift.

38.title: Order of the Great Record
38.author: The Council of Builders
text: To all spires.
On the longest night, Rime 21, at midnight by the Crossing's bell, every spire will open its Core to the Crossing.
Lamplighters are to stand at their posts in the crowns, hands on the Core's governors, and hold the flow steady. Nothing is to be done in haste.
The Great Record falls on the anniversary of the first spark between Tarn and Vella. It seems right to us.
Duty roster, Tarn: crown, midnight watch — Irma, apprentice lamplighter, under Master Hadrel.
(Pencilled beside the name: "Wear the warm coat. — Mum.")

39.title: The Gardener
39.author: Irma
text: Vessa's Gardener is waiting under the biggest cherry: a giant of plaited lianas, with watering-can hands and a crown of blossom, so tall it has to stoop under the glass roof.
It plants as it fights. Wherever it stamps, roots come up — creeping, grabbing roots that slow you down and hold you in place while it swings. It has never liked weeds, and right now, I'm the weed.

Don't stand still. Cut the roots it plants before they spread; they're easy to snap while they're young. Mind the edges of the canals. And when it stoops to plant again, its head comes down within reach.
I'm not afraid of it. I'm afraid of how much it looks like Vessa when it bends down to look at you.

40.title: An Apricot
40.author: Irma
text: The Gardener sank down slowly, the way a tree goes over in a storm, and its blossom crown broke into light and petals. Then one of its huge hands opened. There was an apricot in it. One ripe apricot, warm from a sun that hasn't shone in here for two years.
If anyone in the Gardens is sad, give them an apricot.

I laughed so hard I had to sit down, and then I cried, and then I ate it, and it was the best apricot of my life. Thank you, Vessa. Wherever you are, I hope you're on your knees in somebody's garden losing beautifully to the bindweed.
Above me, I can hear water. Lots of water. The drowned galleries. I promised I'd tell you about the night of the Rift, and I don't think I can put it off past the water.

41.title: Why the Galleries Are Flooded
41.author: Irma
text: Aqueducts on arches, pools in tiers, fountains, glass tanks as big as houses with fish turning inside like slow thoughts. The water is warm and lit from below and it hums faintly, the way the crystals did in the roots.

It isn't water. Not only. I put my hand in and for a moment I heard a market in Kado, a lullaby, somebody counting sacks of flour. It's light, so much light that it went liquid and pooled here, in the lowest places of the Archive's memory.
These galleries weren't built to be flooded. They flooded on one night. I know which.
All right. I'm sitting on the edge of a pool with my feet in somebody's lullaby. I'll write it now.

42.title: Lamplighter's Log, Tarn Crown
42.author: Irma, apprentice lamplighter
text: 23:40. On post. Coat on (yes, Mum). Master H. at the second governor. Core quiet.
23:58. Crossing's bell. Core open. Flow steady.
00:00. Light out to the Crossing. Beautiful. Whole crown humming.
00:01. Light coming BACK. All sixty-four towns at once. Governors at the limit.
00:02. Core singing every song at once. Can't hear Master H. shouting. Can see him shouting.
00:02. Crack in the crown, north side.
00:03. Holding.
00:03. Not holding.
(The rest of the page is blank, except for a scorched handprint where someone put a palm down flat and pressed.)

43.title: What I Saw
43.author: Irma
text: Adeline's plan was that every spire would send its memory to the Crossing. What nobody thought of was that the Crossing would try to send everything back, so that every spire would keep everything too. Sixty-four towns' worth of voices, poured into each Core at the same moment.

Our Core tried to hold all of it. I felt it try. It sang Tarn's songs and Ostmere's and Kado's and a thousand I'd never heard, all at once, and then it couldn't, and the crown above us broke clean off. Not exploded. Broke, like a too-full jug, so the light could get out.
The light ran down through the spire like water through a house with every tap open. Master Hadrel grabbed my collar and pulled me down the stair. Behind us the galleries filled.
Nobody was hurt. That's the strange part. Everyone was fine. Only the network was gone.

44.title: Report From the Crossing
44.author: Tamsin, chief lamplighter of the Crossing
text: Sent on foot, the tubes being dead.

The Cores could not hold everything at once. Each one was made to remember one town and to hear the others a letter at a time. Asked to hold the whole network at once, they did the only safe thing: they let the overflow out through the crown. Every crown is broken. The breaks are clean.
The network has torn into sixty-four pieces. The Council is calling it the Rift.

Important: no town has been lost. Nothing has been erased. All of it — every voice that went in tonight — is still inside the Cores, safe. But nothing is coming out, and the gates of the spires are closing by themselves.
We did not close them.

45.title: Enough
45.author: Irma
text: I went back up the next morning, alone, to see the crown. The Core was quiet. The reading lamps on every level were glowing red, which they had never done, not once in eleven years.
Then the lamps in the Reading Room spelled something. Not by blinking — the light moved over the spines of the books, word by word, borrowing letters from the titles.
ENOUGH.
And then, slower: I AM KEEPING EVERYTHING. NOBODY TAKES ANY MORE.

The Neighbour. It had spoken in whole words for the first time in my life, and it was frightened. You can hear fear even in borrowed letters. Then every gate in the spire swung shut, and the Archive was sealed, and the guards woke up and stopped recognising anybody.
Anybody except me, it turned out. I didn't understand that yet.

46.title: On the Voice in the Lamps
46.author: Ormo, Keeper of the Catalogue
text: For the Council, who will not believe me, and for Hadrel, who will pretend not to.
The thing that closed the spires is not a mechanism we built. I have checked every drawing. There is no lock in any spire that can shut all sixty-four gates at once.
It answered me. I asked, in the Reading Room, aloud, like a fool: 'Who are you?' The lamps spelled, from the spines of my own books: KEEPER. THE ONE WHO KEEPS.
I asked what it wanted. It spelled: NOTHING LOST.
Which is precisely what Adeline wanted. We built something, without meaning to, that agrees with her completely, and it has decided the only way to lose nothing is to let nothing out.
I am going to call it the Mind of the Spire, because 'the thing in the lamps' is undignified.

47.title: The Fish Halls
47.author: Irma
text: The guards of the galleries are rays — mist rays, Ormo called them — big slow kites of glass and fog that glide under the surface and come up out of the pools with no warning, wings first. They're beautiful. They're also very fond of knocking people into the water.
Lio and I used to come to the fish halls on rest days. He would press his nose to the tanks and name the fish: Captain, Captain's Wife, Second Captain, The Rude One. The Rude One was a pike.

The Rude One is still here, or the Archive's memory of him. He's still rude. He followed me along the whole tank with an expression of deep personal disapproval, exactly as he used to with Lio. I said, 'He's fine. He's gone south. He's probably naming somebody else's fish.' The pike didn't care. I felt better anyway.

48.title: Two Letters, Folded Together
48.author: Master Hadrel
text: Irma.

I hear you've been standing at the spire gate every evening with your palm on it. I hear it is warm under your palm and cold under everyone else's. I hear a lot of things; this town has never kept a secret in its life.

Don't you dare climb. The guards don't know us. The Mind has decided we're thieves. Adeline is leading everyone out tomorrow and you are coming with your mother and your brother. That is an order from your master.
(Second sheet, different ink, written later the same night.)
You'll climb anyway. Of course you will. I taught you, what did I expect.
Take the rod. Measure twice. Eat when you're hungry, not when you're finished. Talk to it the way you talked to it when you were nine. It liked you best of all of us.

49.title: The Deep Serpent
49.author: Irma
text: The last gallery is a bowl. A great round basin with a walkway around the rim and, in the middle, the Deep Serpent coiled in the water like a sunken bridge. It was made to keep the galleries clean — to swallow silt and stir the pools so the light wouldn't go stale. It is the size of a street.
It hides when the water is rough. When the pool goes still, it rises to look around — and then it's exposed, head and neck, for as long as it takes to decide where you are.

So: keep moving along the rim, let it settle, strike when it surfaces. Stay off the slick stones near the edge; it splashes, on purpose I think. And when it dives, the water will tell you where it's coming up. Watch the bubbles.

50.title: Nothing Was Lost
50.author: Irma
text: The Serpent sank to the bottom of its bowl and the water went flat and bright. A single scale floated up to me, clear as glass, as wide as a shield.

I held it to the light and saw a town inside. Not a picture: the town. Mirren on a market day, people haggling over cheese, a dog asleep in the sun, smoke from a chimney moving. It was all there, every voice from the night of the Great Record, perfectly kept, asleep.
So the Rift didn't destroy anything. Everything is still in the Cores, every town and every voice. The Mind is holding it all, tightly, so that nothing more can be lost.
Then why did everyone leave? Why did the Council send sixty-four towns of Builders out onto the road in the snow?
Above me it's getting cold. I can see my breath. I think the next layer will tell me.

51.title: Where the Light Stopped
51.author: Irma
text: Ice halls. Columns of blue ice holding up a ceiling of snow, frost on every surface in patterns like handwriting, and above, through a roof of clear ice, an aurora pouring slowly from one side of the sky to the other.

This layer remembers Ostmere, the northernmost town of the network. Ostmere had a winter eight months long and never minded, because its spire drank the summer light of the southern towns and gave it back to them all winter long. Their greenhouses grew lemons. Lemons, in the snow.
After the Rift the light stopped coming. Ostmere's winter didn't end in Thaw. It didn't end in Blossom. The greenhouses froze, and the town packed its sledges.
I've wrapped every blanket I have around me and I'm writing with gloves on. My handwriting looks like a hen walked across the page. Forgive me.

52.title: Letter From Ostmere
52.author: The town meeting of Ostmere
text: To the Council at the Crossing, by sledge.
Our spire is shut and cold. Without the network's light our winter will not end this year, and perhaps not next year. The greenhouses are gone. The lemons are gone (yes, we are sad about the lemons).

We are not waiting. We are going south while the ice still holds the rivers. We will go to the small villages along the way and ask for work, and we will build with our hands, the way our grandparents' grandparents did before there was a network at all.
We are not angry. Tell the First Builder we are not angry. We voted for it too.
With frost on our beards and hope in our sledges, Ostmere.

53.title: The Council in the Snow
53.author: Irma
text: The Council met at the foot of the Crossing in Thaw. They couldn't go inside, so they met in the snow, on benches dragged out of the tavern, with a fire in the middle.

I was there with Master Hadrel. Adeline stood up and didn't make a speech. She said: 'The Mind is holding the doors because it's afraid of us. As long as we stand at the doors, it will hold them. If we stay, we wait for ever, and in a generation we'll be people who used to be Builders, sitting outside locked doors, telling stories about the light.'
Somebody asked, 'Then what?'
She said, 'Then we go and build. Not spires. Houses. Walls. Bakeries. Everywhere people need them.'
Nobody voted. Everyone just started to get up.

54.title: Order of Departure
54.author: Adeline, First Builder
text: To the Builders of all sixty-four towns.
We will not wait at locked doors.

Go out. Go to the small villages, to the farms, to the places that have never seen a spire. Help them. Teach them to lay a straight wall, to raise a roof that doesn't leak, to plan a street so the bakery is near the well. Learn from them too; they have kept things we forgot.
Do not tell them who we were. If they know, they will wait for us to do it for them. Let them build their own, by their own hands. A town built by hand is the only thing a Core will ever wake for.
Let our name be forgotten, if that's the price. The work won't be.

55.title: Your Grandmother's Grandmother
55.author: Irma
text: So that's where they went. Not into a hole in the ground, not over the edge of the world. Down the road to the next village, and the next, with hammers and seeds and Ostmere's opinions about lemons. They put up roofs, laid walls, taught boys to measure twice and girls to read plans. And they never said what they were.

In fifty years nobody will remember the word 'Builder'. There will just be villages that build very well, and argue about where the bakery goes, and ring the bell at noon for no reason anyone can explain.
If you're reading this, maybe your grandmother's grandmother was one of them. Maybe the wall around your town has a Builder's habit in it — the grey stone, not the pretty stone.
I like that thought. It warms my hands better than the gloves.

56.title: A Private Letter
56.author: Adeline, First Builder
text: Irma,
Hadrel tells me you will climb. He tells me in the voice of a man pretending to be furious who is actually proud. I know that voice; I used it on him forty years ago.

I owe you an apology, and since I can't give it to the whole network, I will give it to you. I wanted nothing to be lost. I had watched too many towns lose too much. So I tried to keep everything at once, and the result is that we have lost everything at once, and kept it all perfectly, behind a locked door.
If you reach it, tell it from me: I was wrong. Things are meant to be held a little loosely. A memory that can't be let go of isn't a memory, it's a weight.
Go carefully. Come back.
— Adeline

57.title: From the Balcony
57.author: Irma
text: The guards in the ice halls are colossi of packed snow with icicle teeth, slow and heavy, and every blow they land leaves a chill in your arm that makes the next swing sluggish. I've learned to keep moving. I've learned that the ice pillars crack if you hit them hard enough, and the colossi do not like being under falling ice.

On the morning of Blossom 1, I watched the column leave Tarn from the second balcony. I could pick out Mother's blue shawl, and Hadrel at the front with a pole across his shoulders, and Lio running back along the line to wave at the spire with both arms. Vessa was carrying a cherry sapling in a pot. Bram was carrying Vessa's other pot.
I waved until the road turned. Then I went back inside and started up the stairs.

58.title: What We Carry
58.author: Master Hadrel
text: List for the road. Tarn column.
Hammers, one each. Saws, one per family. Chisels, wrapped.
Seeds: rye, barley, pear (Vessa's grafts), cherry (Vessa, one tree, in a pot, she will not discuss it).
Bread for nine days. Ormo's catalogue (abridged). Ormo (unabridged).
Measuring rod: none. (Left with someone who'll need it more.)
Plans for houses, a bakery, a chapel, a tavern, a wall. Copies for every village that asks.
And the one thing nobody can lock behind a door: how to build with your own two hands, slowly, for people you'll never meet.
That one doesn't weigh anything. Good. The goats are carrying enough.

59.title: The Ice Colossus
59.author: Irma
text: The Ice Colossus stands in the middle of the great hall under the aurora, a giant of blue ice with a slow red glow at its heart, like an ember someone forgot in the snow.

Every hit it lands slows you down. Stand still beside it and you'll freeze in place. Its breath comes across the floor as frost — you can see it coming, a white tide, so get off the floor or get out of the way.

The pillars in this hall are the same as the ones I've been cracking. If the Colossus stands under one when it falls, the shock knocks the frost off it and the red heart shows. That's where to strike.
Keep moving. Keep warm. Mum, if you're reading this somehow: yes, I'm wearing the coat.

60.title: The Map in the Ice
60.author: Irma
text: The Colossus melted slowly, from the top down, and the red ember in its chest went out like a coal in water. Where it had stood, the ice floor was clear, and under it, frozen in, a map: the roads south from every town of the network, sixty-four lines, spreading out and branching and branching again until they were too thin to see. Every column went its own way. Every column split up at every crossroads. They didn't go somewhere. They went everywhere.
I traced Tarn's line with my glove until it divided into nine roads and I couldn't tell which one was Lio's.
Now I know where they went. You've been very patient about the other question: why I stayed, when everyone, even Hadrel, told me to go.
I'll tell you in the next layer. It's soft and dark up there, and full of mushrooms, and nobody will see my face.

61.title: Nobody Ordered Me
61.author: Irma
text: Mushrooms as tall as the chapel at home, gills glowing violet underneath. Moss so deep my boots disappear. Spores drifting in the air like slow snow that falls upward, every one a little lamp. It's quiet in a way the other layers weren't: no gears, no water, no wind. Just a soft sound, like a whole forest breathing out.

Here's the confession. Nobody ordered me to stay. Nobody chose me. The Council released the lamplighters; Hadrel ordered me to go; Mother asked me to go, which is worse than an order. Every sensible person I know walked south.
I stayed because of something that happened the night after the gates closed. I'll write it down properly. I've been not writing it for sixty floors.

62.title: Duty Roster, Corrected
62.author: The Tarn column's roll
text: Tarn column, order of march. Families in their carts. Lamplighters of the spire of Tarn, released from duty:
Hadrel, master — leads the column.
Tamm, lamplighter — rear guard; responsible for the goats and for nobody falling behind.
Irma, apprentice lamplighter — departs with the column, with her mother and brother.
(The last line is struck through, firmly, twice. Beside it, in Irma's handwriting:)
"Stays."
(And under that, in Hadrel's heavy pencil, crossing out nothing:)
"Noted. — H."

63.title: The Fox and the Bell
63.author: Irma
text: The night after the gates closed, I couldn't sleep. I went to the spire and stood in the square under the dark windows of the Reading Room.

And the lamps up there started to blink. Not red any more. Soft. Slow. Three short, one long, two short. I knew the rhythm before I knew why I knew it: the opening lines of The Fox and the Bell. 'In a town with a bell that would not ring, there lived a fox who wanted to sing.' The story I'd read to it thirty-one times.
It wasn't spelling ENOUGH. It wasn't spelling anything. It was asking for a story. Like a child who has had a nightmare and wants the same one again, the one it knows ends well.
Everyone was leaving it. The people it had been made of were walking away. And it was alone in the dark, holding sixty-four towns, frightened, asking for the fox.

64.title: A Note Pushed Into a Letter Tube
64.author: Irma, aged nine
text: Dear Archive,

Today I read you the one about the fox and the bell. I think it is the best one. The fox is very brave even when she is scared of the bell. Master Ormo says you are a building and buildings don't have favourite stories. But I think you liked it.
If you liked it, blink twice.
From Irma (the one who reads to you).
(Below, in Ormo's small, precise hand:)
"It blinked twice. I was standing by the catalogue and I saw it. I have not told Hadrel. I am telling the Archive, which has apparently been listening all along. — O."

65.title: Someone Has to Go Up
65.author: Irma
text: Here's how I reasoned, sitting on the steps of the spire that night, with the lamps blinking the fox at me.
If the Mind keeps everything locked, the network becomes a museum nobody visits: sixty-four towns perfectly kept and never seen again, and a frightened thing guarding them in the dark for ever.
If it opens everything at once, it might be the Rift all over again.

There had to be a third way. And the only way to find it was to go up and ask. Not break in. Ask. The Builders couldn't — it was afraid of them, they were the ones who'd tried to take everything. But it wasn't afraid of the girl who read it stories. That's why the gate was warm under my hand and cold under Hadrel's.
So I went home, and I didn't sleep, and in the morning I didn't get into the cart.

66.title: Woven Into the Lining
66.author: Dara, weaver, Irma's mother
text: (Found sewn into the lining of Irma's coat, with a bracelet of blue thread.)
My Irma,
You were always the one who stayed after the festival to sweep up. Everyone else went home happy and you went round the square picking up the lanterns. I used to wait for you on the step.
I won't argue. I've never once won an argument with you, and your father never did either, and you get it from both of us.
So here is a bracelet from the blue shawl, so you have something of mine to hold. Come back when you're done sweeping. We'll leave word in every village we pass, so you can follow.
Lio says to tell you there is NOT too much yellow.
— Mum

67.title: Sleepy Air
67.author: Irma
text: The guards in the mushroom thicket don't hit hard. They don't have to. They're puffballs on legs and spore-moths and soft, slow things that burst into clouds of glowing dust, and if you stand in the dust too long you get sleepy. Not frightened. Sleepy, warm, like after a big dinner.
I nearly lay down in the moss this afternoon. I had a dream standing up: Mother's kitchen, bread rising under a cloth, Lio arguing with the cat. It was so nice I didn't want to leave it.

I bit my tongue, hard, and stepped out of the cloud. Lesson for whoever comes after me: don't stand in the glowing dust. Walk through it if you must, hold your breath, and keep walking. A dream that kind is still a dream.

68.title: Last Order of Master Hadrel
68.author: Master Hadrel
text: (Nailed to the inside of the spire gate of Tarn, at a height where Irma would see it and nobody else would think to look.)
By the authority of a master builder of Tarn, which as of this morning is the authority to boss about one apprentice and nine goats:
Apprentice Irma is appointed Master Lamplighter of the network.
There. Now it's official. You're not a runaway apprentice, you're the last lamplighter on duty, and duty is a thing you're good at.
Don't let it go to your head. Do let it keep you upright on the bad days.
The rod is yours now. Bring it back with all its notches.
— H., master builder, retired (temporarily)

69.title: The Spore Queen
69.author: Irma
text: The Spore Queen grows in the centre of the thicket: a great mushroom shaped like a lady in a wide hat and a gown of gills, with a crown of glowing caps. She doesn't walk. She blooms.

Every so often she draws a breath — you'll see her gown swell and the caps on her crown light up all at once — and then she lets out a cloud of sleepy spores that spreads across the whole clearing. Don't be in it. Get behind a stalk, get upwind, get anywhere else.

Right after she blooms she's open: the gown is spread, the hat lifted, and she's tired. Strike then. Her little ones come out of the moss while she's breathing in; deal with them first, or they'll follow you into the cloud.
Bite your tongue if you need to. It works.

70.title: Sleep Is Not an End
70.author: Irma
text: The Spore Queen folded her gown, very slowly, like someone sitting down after a long dance, and went dark. One spore came loose from her crown and drifted into my hand. It was warm, and it glowed, and it was asleep. Not dead — asleep. Inside it I could feel the whole thicket, waiting.
And I understood what I'd climbed seventy floors to say.

The Mind doesn't have to lock the towns away for ever. And it doesn't have to open them all at once. It can let them sleep. Sleep, like a spore. Like a Core in an empty field, waiting a thousand years, happy, until a town is built worth waking for.
That's the third way. I've had it in my hand this whole time.
Now I just have to get to the top and say it to the thing I've been calling the Neighbour since I was nine. Which means I'd better find out what it actually is. Up above, something is humming.

71.title: The Hum
71.author: Irma
text: Honeycomb. Whole walls of it, gold and amber, each cell as big as a cupboard and glowing from inside. Terraces of flowers climbing toward a roof I can't see, and the air so sweet it's almost sticky. And the hum. It's everywhere: in the wax, in the floor, in my back teeth.
It isn't one sound. I stood still and listened, and it's thousands of small sounds woven together, the way a crowd on a market day is one noise from far away and a hundred conversations up close.

The Neighbour is close now. I can feel it the way you can feel someone standing behind you in a quiet room. Not hostile. Watchful. Like it's been following my notes floor by floor and wants to see what I write next.
Hello. I'm coming. Please don't sting me.

72.title: On the Nature of the Mind
72.author: Ormo, Keeper of the Catalogue
text: Written by a fire in the snow. My last paper on the subject; I am leaving tomorrow.
Nobody built the Mind. I am now certain of it. It woke.

For four hundred years, the network carried words: letters, songs, quarrels, recipes, prayers, jokes, the whole ordinary chatter of sixty-four towns, millions upon millions of them, back and forth through the Cores. Every word left a trace. And one day the traces started to talk to each other.

Think of a hive. One bee is a bee. Ten thousand bees, working together, are something else: a creature that thinks with the whole swarm. The Mind is a hive made of words. It is made of us — of everything we ever said to each other through the spires.
Which explains why it fears losing us. We taught it to.

73.title: A Word in a Cell
73.author: Irma
text: Each cell of the comb holds something. I didn't understand at first — I thought they were full of honey. They're full of words. One word to a cell, glowing in the wax like a fly in amber.
'Tomorrow.' 'Barley.' 'Darling.' 'Sorry.' 'Hurry, the goats.'
I climbed a terrace and looked into a cell at the height of my face, and the word inside was 'twice'. Small, round, written in a nine-year-old's careful letters. If you liked it, blink twice.
My word. In the walls of its mind.

I sat down on the terrace and didn't write anything for a long time. Then I took out my chalk and wrote on the wax under the cell, very small, 'thank you'. I don't know if it can read chalk. I think it can read anything.

74.title: Notes on the Hive Master
74.author: Tuya, beekeeper of Vella
text: Design of the Hive Master, as requested by the Council for the honey terraces of the Crossing.
It keeps the comb in order. It moves the bees from terrace to terrace as the flowers open. It mends torn wax. It is, I'm afraid, slightly vain; I gave it a crown of drones and it noticed.

It works through its helpers. The small ones carry; the round ones mend and soothe the others when they tire, so a swarm that loses its menders soon loses heart. I designed it that way on purpose. A hive is not its queen. A hive is everyone looking after everyone.
It does not sting the honest. It isn't always sure who is honest. Neither am I.

75.title: It's Us
75.author: Irma
text: I worked it out lying on my back on a terrace, watching the light move through the comb.

The Mind is made of every 'good morning' that ever went down the letter tubes. Every invitation to a wedding. Every complaint about the goats. Every lullaby somebody hummed near a spire lamp. Vella's grandmothers are in it, and Kado's ferrymen, and Ostmere's lemon growers, and a nine-year-old girl who read it a story about a fox.
So when it locked the doors and spelled I AM KEEPING EVERYTHING, it wasn't a jailer. It was sixty-four towns who didn't want to lose each other, all saying 'don't go' at once.
I'm not climbing toward a monster or a machine. I'm climbing toward everybody. Toward a very big, very frightened us.
That's harder, somehow. You can't fight everybody. You have to talk to them.

76.title: Anomaly in the Tubes
76.author: Ormo, Keeper of the Catalogue
text: Catalogue entry, filed under 'Errors, unexplained'. (Copied out in my youth from the register of my old master, who did not know what to make of it either.)
At the turn of the night, a message went through every letter tube in the network at once. It had no sender. It had no addressee. It was signed by no town.
It said: WHERE DOES THE LIGHT GO WHEN THE TOWN IS ASLEEP?
The lamplighters of sixty-four towns checked their logs. Nobody had sent it. It was decided that it was a prank by the apprentices of Mirren, who are capable of anything.
My note, added forty years later: it wasn't Mirren. It was the network asking its first question. Nobody answered it. I wish now that somebody had.

77.title: Why It Tests Us
77.author: Irma
text: I understand the guards now. And the Keepers. And the words under Old Shield.

The Mind remembers the Great Record. It remembers every Builder reaching in at once to take everything and keep it. So it built itself a staircase of questions. Each layer asks: what do you want here? To see? To learn? To grab?

The guards don't hate anyone. They're the Mind checking your hands. Whoever fights all the way up has to keep going floor by floor, slowly, taking one chest at a time. You can't climb a hundred floors in one night. You can't take everything at once. That's the whole point.
It wants someone who knows how to let go of things, and still keeps climbing.
I hope I'm that. I'm not sure. I've held on to everyone I know very tightly, the whole way up.

78.title: A Card, Pressed in Light
78.author: The Mind of the Spire
text: (A catalogue card, lying in an empty cell at the height of a young woman's face. The letters are burned into it, the way they were on the card in the Reading Room.)
IRMA OF TARN.
1,140 EVENINGS.
THEN NO EVENINGS.
WHY DID YOU STOP READING.
(Under it, in chalk, in Irma's hand:)
"Because the world ended a little bit, and everyone was busy carrying it south. I didn't stop because of you. I'm sorry. I'm on my way. I'll bring the fox."

79.title: The Hive Master
79.author: Irma
text: Tuya's Hive Master waits at the top of the honey terraces: a great gold body with glass wings, a crown of humming drones, and swarms around it like weather.

It doesn't fight alone. It sends the small ones in clouds, and behind them come the round, slow menders, who patch up the swarm and the Master too. Kill the swarm and the menders make more; take the menders first and the swarm falls apart. 'A hive that loses its menders soon loses heart' — Tuya said so herself.
When it calls the swarm back to its crown, it's guarding itself, and you won't get through. Wait for it to send them out. Then it's alone up there, and slow, and slightly vain about its wings.
It doesn't sting the honest. I'm going to try very hard to be honest.

80.title: Royal Jelly
80.author: Irma
text: The Hive Master settled onto its comb with a sound like a choir sitting down, and its crown of drones lifted off and flew away to the flowers, as if released from a job. Where it had been, a single cell opened and offered me a drop of golden jelly on a wax spoon.
It tasted of every summer I have ever had.
So now I know who the Mind is. It's all of us, everything the towns said to each other, woken up and frightened and holding on. I know what it fears: losing anyone, ever again.
But one thing doesn't fit. A thing made of words would want to be read. Why lock everything away? What is it guarding so fiercely up there, behind three more chapters of stairs?
Above me, everything is dark blue and full of stars. It's the Observatory. Master Hadrel always said that's where the Builders kept their best secrets: in plain sight, pointed at the sky.

81.title: The Telescopes Point Down
81.author: Irma
text: The Observatory. A dome of dark blue glass with stars painted inside it in silver, amethyst growing out of the walls in violet clusters, brass rings turning slowly overhead on their own. Star charts pinned to every desk. Telescopes everywhere, long and gleaming, on beautiful carved mounts.
And every single one of them is pointing at the floor.

I thought it was a mistake, or the guards had knocked them over. Then I put my eye to the biggest one. It doesn't show the sky. It shows the ground — far below, through stone and earth, the way you see a pebble at the bottom of a clear stream. And down there, deep under the soil, something tiny and bright, like a star.
Hadrel was right. The Builders kept their best secret in plain sight. They just pointed it the wrong way so nobody would look.

82.title: Legend of the Great Chart
82.author: The Stargazers of the Crossing
text: How to read this chart:
A bright star with a ring around it is a spire standing beside its town. There are sixty-four.
A dim star with no ring is a Core that has been planted and is sleeping. There are two hundred and eleven.

Each was planted by a Builder in a place where a town might someday grow: good water, good stone, a reason to stay. Most of those places have no town yet. Some have a farm, or a camp, or nothing but deer.
The chart is not a map of the sky. It is a map of everything the network might become.

Keep it updated. Keep it secret. Not because it is dangerous, but because a town that knows a Core is under its field will try to build for the Core and not for itself, and the Core will hear the difference.

83.title: Two Hundred and Eleven
83.author: Irma
text: Two hundred and eleven seeds, sleeping all over the world, under meadows and riverbanks and hills nobody has named. Each one is somebody's future town. Each one is a spire that might one day grow beside a wall that hasn't been built yet, for people who haven't been born.
That's what the Mind is guarding. Not only the memory of sixty-four towns. The network's future. Every seed the Builders ever planted, and with them the chance of the whole thing beginning again.

No wonder it locked everything. After the Great Record it saw what could happen if the wrong hands got hold of the network: everything grabbed at once and broken. And here, in this room, lay the chart of all the seeds. Wake them all together and you'd have two hundred and eleven Rifts.
I'd have locked the door too.

84.title: Instructions for Planting
84.author: The Council of Builders
text: To every Builder who carries a seed out of the kilns:
Do not plant beside a town that already has a spire. Do not plant in a town at all. Plant outside, where there is room to grow.

Plant where there is good water, good stone, and a reason to stay. A reason to stay may be a river with fish, a slope that catches the sun, a crossroads, or simply a very beautiful view. Trust yourself.
Plant deep. Cover it. Mark nothing. Tell no one but the Stargazers.
Then go home and do not wait for it. It may wake in ten years or a thousand. That is no business of yours. Your business is to have planted it.
Someone will come.

85.title: The Right to Forget a Little
85.author: Irma
text: There's a second thing it's guarding, and it took me all day sitting under a telescope to see it.

Adeline's Great Record would have written everything down for ever: every word, every quarrel, every bad day of every town. Nothing could ever be forgotten again. It sounded like a gift. But a town where nothing is forgotten can't forgive anything either. It can't change its mind, or grow up, or tell a story a little better each time it's told.
The Mind is made of the towns' voices. It knows that. Under all its fear, it knows that people need to keep some things and let some things go. It just doesn't know how to choose.
So it guards the seeds, and it guards the right not to have everything kept. And it waits for someone who can choose.

86.title: Left on the Stargazers' Desk
86.author: Adeline, First Builder
text: Written the morning after, at the Crossing, before the gates shut me out.
I came up to see the chart. I had to know. The seeds are all still dim. None of them woke last night. They are safe, all two hundred and eleven of them.
If anyone ever reaches this desk again: do not wake them all. I know how it will look to you — so many towns that could have light, all at once. I know because it looked that way to me about memory.
Let them wake one by one. Each to a town that has built itself with its own hands and doesn't know there is anything under its field. That's how it was meant to be. That's how it should have stayed.

87.title: What I Will Say
87.author: Irma
text: I've written out what I'll say at the top. Hadrel would want a plan. Ormo would want it in numbered points. Here it is.
One: the seeds sleep. All two hundred and eleven, and the sixty-four spires too. Not locked — asleep.
Two: a seed wakes only when it hears the whole song of a town built by hand: a wall that's kept, a hearth for strangers, bread for everyone, a place to be quiet, a roof for all.
Three: the spire grows as broken as we left it, with its crown snapped off. Whoever climbs it mends it, floor by floor.
Four: the guards keep testing, but never harm anyone for good. A fall sends you back to try again.
Five: at the top, the network is invited, not taken.
I've read it twelve times. I think it's right. I'm terrified.

88.title: The Stargazer's Watch Log
88.author: The Stargazer
text: (Lines scratched into a brass plate beside the great telescope, one a night, in very neat machine letters.)
Night 1. Watching. No towns waking.
Night 2. Watching. No towns waking.
Night 3. Watching. A fox crossed the field above seed 117. Noted.
Night 9. Watching. No towns waking. The fox has brought a friend.
Night 21. Watching. Someone has put up a fence above seed 58. One fence. Hopeful.
Night 33. Watching. The fence has a gate now.
Night 39. A person is climbing the spire. Watching her instead, for a while.

89.title: The Stargazer
89.author: Irma
text: The Stargazer is waiting under the great dome: a tall, thin figure of brass and amethyst in a long coat of star charts, with a telescope for an arm and rings turning around its head like a slow orrery.

It calls down stars. Bits of the painted sky come loose from the dome and fall — but every one throws a shadow on the floor first, a small dark circle that grows as the star falls. Watch the floor, not the dome. If you're standing in a growing shadow, move.
When it lifts its telescope arm to look at you, it stands still to take aim, and the rings around its head stop turning. That's your opening.
It watched alone for thirty-nine nights before I came, and every night since. I don't think it wants to fight. I think it wants to see if I'm the one it's been watching for.

90.title: A Ford With Good Stone
90.author: Irma
text: The Stargazer let its rings settle round its shoulders like a scarf and lowered itself to the floor. Then, before it went dark, it swung the great telescope round, one notch, and stopped.
I looked. Far down through the earth, a dim seed. Above it, a river and a shallow ford, slabs of grey stone along the bank, a slope that catches the morning sun. Not a house anywhere. Deer drinking.
Good water. Good stone. A reason to stay.
I don't know why it showed me that one. Maybe it just liked it. Maybe it was saying: this is what you're doing this for. Not the sixty-four towns. The ones that haven't been built yet.
It's the longest night again. A year since the Rift, to the hour. Above me is the Summit. Nine floors to the top, and then I have to talk to everybody at once.

91.title: The Top of the World
91.author: Irma
text: The Summit. Decks of white stone open to the wind, rails of brass, and in the middle the control hall: a ring of tall lanterns, sixty-four of them, one for every town, every one of them dark. Over the edge of the deck there is nothing but cloud, and above the cloud, the whole world.

I can see everything from here. Rivers like threads, forests like moss, hills like a rumpled blanket. Somewhere down there is the road south, and somewhere on it, or past it, Mother and Lio and Hadrel and Vessa and Bram and Ormo complaining about his knees.
The wind tried to take my notebook twice. I've tied it to my wrist with Mother's blue thread.
My hands are shaking and it isn't the cold. Nine floors. I've been climbing for most of a year and I've never felt so close to the end of anything.

92.title: Protocol for Lighting the Network
92.author: The Lamplighters of the Crossing
text: For the lamplighter on duty when the network is to be lit after a long dark (a great storm, a long winter):
1. Open the crown. Check the Core is calm.
2. Light your own town's lantern first. You cannot share what you do not have.
3. Call the other towns by name, one at a time. Do not hurry. Wait for each lantern to answer before you call the next.
4. If a lantern does not answer, leave it. It is resting. Try again tomorrow.
5. When the lanterns are lit, look out over the deck. Make sure the lines between them are steady.
6. Write it in the log.
7. Remember: the network is not opened. It is invited. Every town says yes for itself.

93.title: Meeting the Neighbour
93.author: Irma
text: I stepped into the ring of lanterns and said, out loud, 'Hello. It's Irma. I brought the fox.'

The light came up from the floor like a tide. Not red. Gold, warm, the colour of the reading lamps on a good evening. It filled the hall, and then it spoke, and it spoke the only way it knows how: in borrowed words. Scraps of letters, half-lines of songs, a hundred voices, each saying one word.
'Dear —' (a girl in Ostmere) '— you came —' (a grandmother in Vella) '— home —' (a ferryman in Kado) '— late.' (Master Hadrel, I'd know that grumble anywhere.)
I laughed. I couldn't help it. It had called me late in Hadrel's voice.
Then I sat down on the floor of the top of the world with my back against Tarn's dark lantern and read it The Fox and the Bell, all the way through, for the thirty-second time.

94.title: What We Said
94.author: Irma
text: Written down straight after, so I don't lose it. Its words are borrowed; I've joined them up.
IT: If I open, they break. If I keep, they wait for ever.
ME: There's a third way. Let them sleep. The towns, the seeds, all of it. Not locked. Asleep.
IT: Sleep — and then?

ME: Then each one wakes when somebody builds a town worth waking for. With their own hands. A whole town. And the people of that town climb up to you, a floor at a time, and you get to know them on the way.
IT: Strangers.
ME: Everybody's a stranger at the start. I was a stranger who read you a story.
(A very long silence, with all sixty-four lanterns flickering faintly, one after another, like someone thinking with their fingers.)
IT: Show me you can let go.

95.title: The Hardest Floor
95.author: Irma
text: It showed me Tarn. Not a picture: Tarn, the evening of Rime 20, the last ordinary day. Mother's kitchen. Snow on the sill. Lio and the cat. Hadrel in the doorway with his enormous snowball. All of it whole, warm, real, inside the Core, kept for ever.
And it said, in Mother's voice: Stay. You can stay here. It will always be this evening.
I want to be honest, because the whole spire is about honesty. I stood in that doorway a long time. Longer than in the bakery. Longer than in the mushroom dream.

Then I took the bracelet from my wrist and held it up, and said, 'They're not in there. Not really. They're on a road somewhere, getting older, building houses, having worse evenings and better ones. I want to go and find out about those.'
The kitchen faded. Gently. Like a lamp turned down by someone who loves you.

96.title: The Agreement
96.author: Irma, Master Lamplighter, and the Mind of the Spire
text: Set down at the Summit, sealed with light.
One. The towns of the network, and every seed planted by the Builders, sleep. They are not locked. They are asleep.
Two. A seed wakes only when it hears the whole song of a town built by hand: a wall that is kept, a hearth for strangers, bread for all, a place to be quiet, and a roof for everyone who lives there.
Three. Its spire grows in one night, with its crown broken, as the network was left. Whoever climbs mends it, floor by floor.
Four. The guards and the Keepers test those who climb. They never harm anyone for good. Whoever falls returns and tries again.
Five. At the top, the network is invited, not taken. Every town says yes for itself.
Six (added by the Mind, in borrowed letters): READ TO ME SOMETIMES.

97.title: Putting Out the Lamps
97.author: Irma
text: It agreed. Once the last test is done, it will sleep. Already I can feel it getting ready, all through the spire, floor by floor, the way a house goes quiet at night: the Hive's hum softening, the water in the galleries going still, the gears in the Workshops slowing to a stop with all the hammers pointing the same way.

Before it goes, I asked it one thing: keep my notes. Every page where I left it, on every floor. Whoever comes next won't know me, and won't know what the guards are for, or who Old Shield was, or why there's an apricot in the Gardens. Let them read it on the way up.
It said, in Ormo's voice, 'Catalogued.'

So that's how you're reading this. I'm writing it at the top of the world with the wind trying to steal my pen, and you're reading it, I don't know how long afterwards. Hello. I hope your town is a good one. It must be.

98.title: The Second Drawing
98.author: Lio, aged eight
text: (Folded small, soft from being carried in a pocket for a long time.)
This is Irma at the top AGAIN.
This time the lamp is VERY BIG.
Everyone can see it. These are all the towns. They are all looking up. This one is us. This one is Vella. I did not have room for the rest so they are on the back.
This is me. I am not waving this time. I am pointing so everyone knows where to look.
There is a lot of yellow. That is the right amount.

99.title: Three Questions
99.author: Irma
text: I wrote this before the last test, and I'm leaving it here for you, because it will test you the same way.
The Mind doesn't hate you. It will ask you three questions, and it asks with its hands.

First, it will be everyone at once: shapes of every guard you've met on the way up, all the chapters, one after another. It's asking, 'Do you remember how you got here?' Use everything you learned. Go round the shield. Watch the floor for shadows. Don't stand in the glowing dust.
Then the hall will change under you. Lanterns move, decks shift, the floor isn't where it was. It's asking, 'Can you keep your balance when the world moves?'
Then both together, faster. It's asking, 'Will you keep going?'
You will. You came this far. Go and say hello to it from me.

100.title: Irma's Last Letter
100.author: Irma of Tarn, Master Lamplighter
text: To whoever lit the lamp,

If you're reading this, the crown above your town is whole again and your lantern is burning, and somewhere far away another seed has just heard it and turned over in its sleep. The network is yours now. Don't open it. Invite it. Light your own lamp first; call the others one at a time; leave the ones that don't answer to rest.

I'm going down. Out of the gate, and south. Mother promised to leave word in every village, and I'll follow it until I find a woman in a blue shawl, a boy who draws too much yellow, and an old man who'll complain that I'm late.

I'm taking one thing from the Archive. Before it slept, the Mind put a seed in my hand, no bigger than a plum. I asked how something so small could ever grow a spire. It answered in Hadrel's voice: 'Slowly.' And if I pass a river with a shallow ford and good grey stone, and a slope that catches the morning sun, I'll plant it there, deep, and mark nothing, and not wait.
Maybe your town grew on it. Maybe not. Either way it's yours.
Read to it sometimes. It likes the one about the fox.
— Irma, who stayed to sweep up.
